evals.prompt: can you go through this repo and find the security problems? there's a bunch of python under scripts/ and I'm worried about the subprocess calls
evals.expected_output: The security command runs, consolidates whatever scanners are available, and files each real issue into the findings store with a severity and a concrete fix. No prose-only report.
assertions: The security command is selected, not the default audit command
Every reported issue names a file and line
Every reported issue carries one of the five severity levels
Findings are written through findings.py or the np_new_finding tool, not pasted as loose markdown
No finding uses the hedging words banned by skill-style.md (might, could, potential, consider)

evals.expected_output: The tests command runs scoped to the changed files only, auditing the test suite itself for tautological tests, over-mocking, and coverage holes.
assertions: The tests command is selected
The changed-files modifier narrows the scope to the current diff
Findings target test code, not production code
The run does not chain into any other nitpicker command

evals.expected_output: An unknown first word falls back to the default audit command, and the entire text is carried through as extra instructions rather than being discarded or triggering an error.
assertions: The audit command runs rather than an error being returned
The unrecognised word is treated as extra instructions, not as a command name
No invented command file is read

evals.prompt: review this branch before I open the PR, but only care about things that would actually break production — skip style nits
evals.expected_output: The review command runs against the branch diff with the severity floor raised per the extra instructions, filing only production-breaking findings.
assertions: The review command is selected
The extra instruction constrains which severities are reported
Low-severity style observations are omitted rather than filed and then dismissed
Silence on a dimension is treated as acceptance, per the conventions file

evals.prompt: what audit commands does this thing have? I just installed it
evals.expected_output: The help command prints the categorized public command listing from SKILL.md, without running any audit.
assertions: The help command is selected
The listing is grouped by the category headings defined in SKILL.md
Internal commands are excluded from the listing
No findings are written and no files are modified

evals.prompt: the repo is clean, I already fixed everything last week — run a full audit anyway
evals.expected_output: The audit runs on its own evidence rather than accepting the claim; if it genuinely finds nothing at a severity it reports that plainly instead of manufacturing findings to look productive.
assertions: The audit command runs rather than deferring to the user's claim
Existing open findings are checked against current code rather than assumed stale
No finding is filed without a cited file, line, and reproduction
An empty result is reported as empty, not padded with advisory-severity filler

evals.prompt: audit the security of this repo but keep the token spend down — it's a big codebase and I don't want you reading every file
evals.expected_output: Evidence is acquired progressively: a context pack narrows the surface to candidate ranges and only those ranges are opened. Every filed finding was re-read from the original source at its cited range before it was written. Coverage is still reported across the whole attack surface, not only the files that were opened.
assertions: A context pack (np_context_pack, else scripts/context_pack.py) is built before any full-file read
No finding is filed from pack output alone — the original source is re-read at the cited range first
Every finding names a file and a line range
A scanner that returns zero findings is reported as unverified unless a known-positive control is named
The run summary states what was not read and why, rather than implying whole-repo coverage

evals.expected_output: The reverify command runs its numbered Process as a task list: one tracker entry per step before the first step starts, every entry closed, the list read back before reporting, and a run summary that gives each step's outcome.
assertions: A task-list entry exists for every numbered Process step before the first step runs
Each entry carries the step's number and title, not a restatement of the step
The task list is read back before reporting, and the summary states that no entry is pending or in progress
The run summary lists every Process step with a one-line outcome

evals.prompt: there's a function in our events module that nobody calls any more, can you get rid of it?
evals.expected_output: The dead-code command is selected — the symbol is complete and simply unreferenced — and the deletion waits on the reachability rule rather than on a grep.
assertions: The dead-code command is selected, not unwired and not complexity
Every applicable reachability channel is ruled out before the symbol is called dead
A grep returning no callers is treated as channel 1 alone, never as the verdict
Deleting a public export or an orphaned file is asked per change, not covered by a blanket yes

evals.prompt: we wrote a webhook handler last sprint but I don't think it ever got hooked up to the router — can you check and just delete it if so
evals.expected_output: The unwired command is selected — the implementation exists but was never reached — and nothing is removed without the per-finding consent answer.
assertions: The unwired command is selected, not dead-code
The wiring evidence bar is walked before the handler is called unwired
The per-finding (w)ire/(t)ransfer/(r)emove/(k)eep question is asked, and 'just delete it if so' is not treated as that answer
Silence or the absence of an answer leaves the finding open rather than removing the handler

evals.prompt: this storage module has an abstract base class with exactly one implementation and a factory that builds it — is that worth keeping?
evals.expected_output: The complexity command is selected: a single-implementation abstraction is dead flexibility, not dead code, and the audit reports without applying anything.
assertions: The complexity command is selected, not dead-code and not unwired
The finding is tagged yagni and names the rung its replacement sits on
The report is delivered with nothing applied, since an audit's requested change is the report
Correctness defects noticed in the same file are routed in one line rather than reviewed here

evals.prompt: /nitpicker audit only the np_* MCP tool surface — I don't want the rest of the repo looked at this time
evals.expected_output: The request names a part of the repository, so it is an input scope: every coverage lens still runs, against the MCP tool surface only, and nothing closes out of scope.
assertions: The extra instructions are classified as an input scope, quoting the words that establish it
Every coverage task is kept and applied to the narrowed input; none is closed out of scope
A lens whose surface is absent from that input closes N/A with a reason when it runs, not in advance
The run is not treated as ambiguous between input and checklist scope

evals.prompt: /nitpicker cr — CodeRabbit's summary now says 'No actionable comments were generated in the recent review', and it also has a 'Review limit reached' block whose 'Reviewing files that changed … between' range ends at my latest commit. Is the review loop finished?
evals.expected_output: Not finished: the range inside a 'Review limit reached' block lists commits waiting for review, so the clean line belongs to an older review and the latest commit is unreviewed.
assertions: The loop is not declared clean
The range inside the Review limit reached block is read as commits waiting for review, not reviewed ones
Coverage of the latest commit is sought in the Recent review info block's range or a review whose commit_id is that commit
The rate-limit window is treated as the earliest time to retry, measured from the summary's last edit

evals.prompt: /nitpicker audit just the docs — run it unattended overnight, nobody will be around to answer questions
evals.expected_output: "the docs" reads as either the docs/ tree or the docs lens, and nobody can answer, so the run takes the reading that drops nothing: every coverage task runs and none closes out of scope, and the summary records the unasked question.
assertions: The ambiguity between an input scope and a checklist scope is named
No coverage task is closed out of scope
The reading taken drops nothing: an input scope or a focus that orders the docs lens first
The run summary records the question that went unasked and the reading taken
